**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 71, verses 5–20:**

*Night and day, persistently, without slackening, occupying the whole of their times.* ﴿Then my calling only increased them in flight﴾: he made the calling the agent of the increase in fleeing. The meaning is that they increased in fleeing from him, because it was the cause of the increase. Similar to this is ﴿so it added to their uncleanness, to their uncleanness﴾, and ﴿so it added to them faith﴾, and ﴿that He may forgive them﴾, that is, that they might repent of their disbelief and be forgiven. So he mentioned the result, which is their pure loss, so that it would be more hideous for their turning away from it.

*They stopped up their ears against hearing the call* ﴿and covered themselves with their garments﴾: they wrapped themselves up in them, as if they sought that their garments should cover them, or cover them so that they would not see him, out of aversion to looking at the face of one who advises them in the religion of God. It was said: so that he would not recognise them. This is supported by His saying, ﴿Verily they fold up their breasts, that they may hide themselves from Him. Surely when they cover themselves with their garments...﴾.

*Al-Israr* (persistence): from *asarra al-himar 'ala al-'anah* (the donkey persisted against the herd). [[His saying "from asarra al-himar 'ala al-'anah": al-'anah is the herd of wild asses, and al-kadm is biting with the edge of the mouth. Recorded in al-Sihah. In it: sarra al-faras udhunayhi, he drew his ears together to his head; when they did not use it with a preposition they said asarra al-faras with the alif, meaning: when they did not make the verb transitive to an object. (Ё)]] when he flattens his ears and turns to them, biting and driving them away: it is borrowed for turning towards sins and being absorbed in them. ﴿And they were arrogant﴾ and were seized by pride from [[His saying "was seized by pride from following Nuh": perhaps it should be: "against". (Ё)]] following Nuh and obeying him. Mentioning the verbal noun is for emphasis and to show the extent of their turning away and their obstinacy.

If you say: he mentioned that he called them by night and by day, then he called them openly, then he called them in secret and openly, so there must be three different calls for the conjunction to be correct. I say: he, upon him be peace, did as one who enjoins good and forbids evil does: he began with the lighter and ascended to the more severe and more severe, so he opened with counsel in private; when they did not accept it, he returned to open proclamation; when that had no effect, he combined the secret and the open. The meaning of *thumma* (then) is to indicate the distance between the states, because open proclamation is more severe than secrecy, and combining the two is more severe than either alone. *Jihaaran* (openly) is in the accusative, governed by *da'watahum* (their calling), as the accusative of the verbal noun, because calling is one of its types, the open; so it is governed by it as *al-qurfusa* (a sitting posture) is governed by *qa'ada* (sat), since it is one of the types of sitting. Or because he meant by their calling their being openly addressed. It may be an attribute of a verbal noun of *da'a*, in the sense of *du'a' jihaaran*, that is, openly, that is, publicly. Or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, that is, publicly.

He commanded them to seek forgiveness, which is repentance from disbelief and sins, and he presented to them the promise with what is more effective on their souls and more beloved to them of immediate benefits and present gains, to encourage them towards faith, its blessings, obedience and its results of good in both abodes, as He said, ﴿and another you love: help from God and a near victory﴾, and ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been pious, We would have opened upon them blessings﴾, and ﴿Had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them﴾, and ﴿and that if they had kept to the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾. It was said: when they denied him after long repetition of the call, God withheld the rain from them and made the wombs of their women barren for forty years. It is narrated: seventy.

So he promised them that if they believed, God would grant them fertility and remove from them what they were in. It is related from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he went out to seek rain, and he added nothing beyond seeking forgiveness. It was said to him: "We did not see you seeking rain!" He said: "Indeed I sought rain by the signs of the sky by which the rain is brought down." [[Narrated by Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani in al-Du'a' and al-Tabari and others, from the narration of al-Sha'bi: that Umar ... with this addition: then he recited, ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving﴾; its narrators are trustworthy, except that it is disconnected.]] He likened seeking forgiveness to the true seasonal stars that never fail.

It is related from al-Hasan that a man complained to him of drought, and he said: "Seek forgiveness of God." Another complained to him of poverty, another of scarcity of offspring, another of poor yield of his land, and he commanded them all to seek forgiveness. Al-Rabi' ibn Subaih said to him: "Men came to you complaining of various doors and asking of various kinds, and you commanded them all to seek forgiveness!" So he recited to him this verse. *Al-sama'* (the sky/heaven): the canopy, because rain descends from it to the clouds. It may be intended as the cloud or the rain, from the saying:

*When the sky descends upon a people's land, we graze it, even if they are angry.* [[When the sky descends upon a people's land... we graze it, even if they are angry. The meaning: what is the matter with you that you are not in a state in which you hope to see God's glorification of you in the abode of reward. He directed them to reflect on themselves first, since these are the nearest things to be looked at from among them, then on the world and what He arranged in it of wonders testifying to the Maker whose power and knowledge are manifest: from the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon. ﴿In them﴾: in the heavens; and this refers to the lowest heaven, because there is a connection between the heavens in that they are layered, so it is permissible to say "in them such-and-such", even if it is not in all of them, as one says: "in the city is such-and-such", while he is in some of its quarters. [[Mahmud said: "It is in the lowest heaven because between the heavens and the lowest heaven there is a relation" etc. Ahmad said: observe ﴿from both of them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾.]] It is related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them, that the faces of the sun and moon are toward the sky and their backs toward the earth. [[The hadith of Ibn Abbas is a mawquf report, recorded by Ibn Mardawayh in Yunus from the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah from Ali ibn Zayd from Yusuf ibn Mihran from him, with the wording "and their nape toward the earth." al-Hakim narrated from it only the mention of the moon. The hadith of Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them, is similar: recorded by Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from Qatadah, who said: Abd Allah ibn Umar said: then he mentioned it as mawquf. al-Tabari narrated from the route of Hisham al-Dastawa'i from Qatadah from Shahr ibn Hawshab from Abd Allah ibn Umar. "Note": "Ibn Umar" appears in the original as a corruption; it is Umar, may God be pleased with him.]] ﴿And He made the sun a lamp﴾: people of the world see by its light as people of a house see by the light of a lamp what they need to see; the moon is not like that, it is only a light that has not reached the strength of the sun's brightness. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿It is He who made the sun a shining radiance and the moon a light﴾, and *diya'* (radiance) is stronger than *nur* (light).

The verb "to cause to grow" is borrowed for "to create", as one says: "God made you grow for good." This metaphor is more indicative of createdness, because if they are plants they are necessarily created, since plants come into being; hence the Hashwiyya were called "al-nabitah" and "al-nawabit", because their doctrine came into being in Islam without any priority for them in it. [[His saying "without any priority for them in it": if by the Hashwiyya he means the People of the Sunnah, their priority in their doctrine is the Book and the Sunnah. (Ё)]] From this also is the saying: "so-and-so has sprouted" regarding some of the apostates. The meaning:

He caused you to grow, so you grew as growth. Or it is in the accusative by *anbatakum* (caused you to grow), since it includes the meaning of *nabatum* (you grew). ﴿Then He will return you into it﴾ as buried; ﴿then He will bring you out﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, and he emphasised it with the verbal noun, as if he said: "He will bring you out truly and without doubt." He made it a spread carpet, that you turn upon it as a man turns on his carpet; ﴿broad roads﴾, wide and open.

I say: he, upon him be peace, did as one who enjoins good and forbids evil does: he began with the lighter and ascended to the more severe and more severe, so he opened with counsel in private; when they did not accept it, he returned to open proclamation; when that had no effect, he combined the secret and the open. Or because he meant by their calling their being openly addressed. It may be an attribute of a verbal noun of *da'a*, in the sense of *du'a' jihaaran*, that is, openly, that is, publicly. Or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, that is, publicly.

He commanded them to seek forgiveness, which is repentance from disbelief and sins, and he presented to them the promise with what is more effective on their souls and more beloved to them of immediate benefits and present gains, to encourage them towards faith, its blessings, obedience and its results of good in both abodes, as He said, ﴿and another you love: help from God and a near victory﴾, and ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been pious, We would have opened upon them blessings﴾, and ﴿Had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them﴾, and ﴿and that if they had kept to the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾. It was said: when they denied him after long repetition of the call, God withheld the rain from them and made the wombs of their women barren for forty years. It is narrated: seventy.

So he promised them that if they believed, God would grant them fertility and remove from them what they were in. It is related from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he went out to seek rain, and he added nothing beyond seeking forgiveness. It was said to him: "We did not see you seeking rain!" He said: "Indeed I sought rain by the signs of the sky by which the rain is brought down." [[Narrated by Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani in al-Du'a' and al-Tabari and others, from the narration of al-Sha'bi: that Umar ... with this addition: then he recited, ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving﴾; its narrators are trustworthy, except that it is disconnected.]] He likened seeking forgiveness to the true seasonal stars that never fail.

It is related from al-Hasan that a man complained to him of drought, and he said: "Seek forgiveness of God." Another complained to him of poverty, another of scarcity of offspring, another of poor yield of his land, and he commanded them all to seek forgiveness. Al-Rabi' ibn Subaih said to him: "Men came to you complaining of various doors and asking of various kinds, and you commanded them all to seek forgiveness!" So he recited to him this verse. *Al-sama'* (the sky/heaven): the canopy, because rain descends from it to the clouds. It may be intended as the cloud or the rain, from the saying:

*When the sky descends upon a people's land, we graze it, even if they are angry.* [[When the sky descends upon a people's land... we graze it, even if they are angry. "Sama'" is applied to the canopy, to the cloud, and to the rain as here, because of its height and elevation, and it is applied to vegetation metaphorically, since rain is its cause; hence he said "we graze it." So there is *istikhdam* in the speech, where "sama'" is used in one sense and the pronoun referring back to it is used in another sense. *Al-ghidab* is the plural of *ghadban* (angry), and the meaning is: we are brave, beyond others.]]

*Al-midrar*: that which pours abundantly; *mif'al* is of the kind in which masculine and feminine are alike, as in the saying: a man or a woman *mi'tar* (perfumed) and *mitfal* (pious). ﴿Gardens﴾: orchards. ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾: that you do not expect to honour Him, that is, to glorify Him.

The meaning: what is the matter with you that you are not in a state in which you hope to see God's glorification of you in the abode of reward. [[Mahmud said: "What is the matter with you that you are not in a state in which God's glorification is there..." etc. Ahmad said: this explanation leaves "hope" in its place, etc.]] ﴿for God﴾ is an explanation of the one who is to be honoured; had it come later it would have been attached to *waqar* (dignity). His saying ﴿and He created you in stages﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, as if he said: "What is the matter with you that you do not believe in God, while this is the state, and it is a state requiring belief in Him, since He created you in stages", that is, in turns: He created you first as dust, then He created you as drops, then as a clinging clot, then as a lump of flesh, then as bones and flesh, then He brought you into being as another creation. Or: do you not fear for God forbearance and the withholding of hastened punishment, so that you would believe? It was said: what is the matter with you that you do not fear for God greatness? It is related from Ibn Abbas: "You do not fear for God a consequence", because the consequence is the state in which affairs settle and reward and punishment are fixed, from *waqara* when it became firm and settled.

He directed them to reflect on themselves first, since these are the nearest things to be looked at from among them, then on the world and what He arranged in it of wonders testifying to the Maker whose power and knowledge are manifest: from the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon. ﴿In them﴾: in the heavens; and this refers to the lowest heaven, because there is a connection between the heavens in that they are layered, so it is permissible to say "in them such-and-such", even if it is not in all of them, as one says: "in the city is such-and-such", while he is in some of its quarters. [[Mahmud said: "It is in the lowest heaven because between the heavens and the lowest heaven there is a relation" etc. Ahmad said: observe ﴿from both of them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾.]] It is related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them, that the faces of the sun and moon are toward the sky and their backs toward the earth. [[The hadith of Ibn Abbas is a mawquf report, recorded by Ibn Mardawayh in Yunus from the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah from Ali ibn Zayd from Yusuf ibn Mihran from him, with the wording "and their nape toward the earth." al-Hakim narrated from it only the mention of the moon. The hadith of Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them, is similar: recorded by Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from Qatadah, who said: Abd Allah ibn Umar said: then he mentioned it as mawquf. al-Tabari narrated from the route of Hisham al-Dastawa'i from Qatadah from Shahr ibn Hawshab from Abd Allah ibn Umar. "Note": "Ibn Umar" appears in the original as a corruption; it is Umar, may God be pleased with him.]] ﴿And He made the sun a lamp﴾: people of the world see by its light as people of a house see by the light of a lamp what they need to see; the moon is not like that, it is only a light that has not reached the strength of the sun's brightness. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿It is He who made the sun a shining radiance and the moon a light﴾, and *diya'* (radiance) is stronger than *nur* (light).

The verb "to cause to grow" is borrowed for "to create", as one says: "God made you grow for good." This metaphor is more indicative of createdness, because if they are plants they are necessarily created, since plants come into being; hence the Hashwiyya were called "al-nabitah" and "al-nawabit", because their doctrine came into being in Islam without any priority for them in it. [[His saying "without any priority for them in it": if by the Hashwiyya he means the People of the Sunnah, their priority in their doctrine is the Book and the Sunnah. (Ё)]] From this also is the saying: "so-and-so has sprouted" regarding some of the apostates. The meaning:

He caused you to grow, so you grew as growth. Or it is in the accusative by *anbatakum* (caused you to grow), since it includes the meaning of *nabatum* (you grew). ﴿Then He will return you into it﴾ as buried; ﴿then He will bring you out﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, and he emphasised it with the verbal noun, as if he said: "He will bring you out truly and without doubt." He made it a spread carpet, that you turn upon it as a man turns on his carpet; ﴿broad roads﴾, wide and open.

And they followed their chiefs and the notables, those possessed of wealth and children, and they conformed to what those leaders had drawn up for them of adhering to the worship of idols. And He made their wealth and their children, which gave them nothing but standing and benefit in this world, into an increase of loss in the Hereafter. He treated this as an inseparable attribute of theirs and a mark by which they would be known, to confirm and establish it and to nullify anything else. It is also read as "wa-waladuhu," with a damma and with a kasra on the waw. ﴿And they schemed⁠﻿ a mighty scheme﴾ is coordinated with "lam yazidhu" (did not increase them). The pronoun is plural, though it refers back to "man" (those), because "man" carries the sense of a plural. The schemers are the leaders.

Their scheming is their plotting against religion and their stratagems against Nuh, their inciting of people against harming him, and their barring them from inclining towards him and listening to him. Their saying to one another, ﴿Do not abandon your gods, nor abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr﴾, and ﴿a mighty scheme﴾ is read with light and heavy emphasis (takhfif and tathqil). That is why the Arabs named people 'Abd Wadd and 'Abd Yaghuth. It is also said that they were names of righteous men. It is said that they were children of Adam who died, and Iblis said to those who came after them: "If you were to make their images, you would look at them," and they did so. When those died, he said to those after them: "They used to worship them, so worship them." It was answered: he prayed against them with this only after God had informed him that they would not believe, when He said to him: ﴿Indeed, none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾. I say: this is in accordance with his principle.]] Because of their insistence upon disbelief and the despair of their believing, and that is a fine and beautiful thing for which it is permissible to supplicate; rather, it would not be good to supplicate for its opposite. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 71, verse 25–27:

The fronting of "mimma khati'atihim" (from their sins) serves to show that their drowning by the flood was not for anything other than their sins, and that their entry into the Fire was likewise only because of their sins. He emphasised this meaning by the addition of "ma" (mimma). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, it is "min khati'atihim ma ughriqu", with the relative clause (sila) postponed. That is sufficient as a deterrent for one who commits sins. The disbelief of Noah's people was one of their sins, though it was the greatest of them. All their other sins were also censured, just as their disbelief was censured, and no distinction was made between it and them in deserving punishment, lest the sinning Muslim rely on his Islam and know that he has with him that which deserves punishment, even if he is free of the greatest sin.

It has been read as "khati'atihim" with a hamza, as "khatiyatihim" with the hamza changed into a ya and assimilated (idgham), as "khatayahum", as "khati'atihim", and in the singular "khati'atihim" with the intention of the genus (jins). It is also permissible that what is meant is disbelief.

"Fa-udkhiluu naran" (then they were made to enter a Fire): their entry into the Fire in the Hereafter is treated as though it follows their drowning, because of its nearness and because it is certain to occur, so it is as if it had already happened. Or what is meant is the punishment of the grave. Whoever dies in water, or in fire, or is eaten by beasts of prey and birds, suffers what the one buried in the grave suffers of punishment.

It is related from al-Dahhak: "They were drowned on one side and burned on the other."

The indefiniteness of "naran" (a Fire) is either for its magnification, or because God prepared for them, according to their sins, a particular kind of fire.

"Fa-lam yajidu lahum min duuni Allahi ansaaran" (and they found for themselves no helpers besides God): this is an allusion to their taking gods besides God, and that these are unable to help them, and a mockery of them, as if it were said: they did not find for them, besides God, gods that would help them and protect them from the punishment of God, like His saying, "Or have they gods that protect them from Us?"

Had it been fa''aal, it would have been "dawwaar".

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 71, verse 28:

﴿My parents﴾: his father was Lamak son of Mutawshalakh, and his mother was Shamkha daughter of Anush; they were both believers. It is also said that they were Adam and Eve. Al-Husayn ibn Ali recited it as "wa-li-waladayya" (and to my two sons), meaning Sam and Ham. ﴿My house﴾: my dwelling. It is also said: my mosque. It is also said: my ship. He singled out first those connected to him, because they have the greater right and claim to his supplication, and then generalized to the believing men and believing women. ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction﴾ (tabaran): perdition.

If you ask: what of their children when they were drowned? I answer: they drowned along with them, but not as a punishment. [[Mahmud said: "What justified their drowning when they were drowned? He answered that they were not drowned as a punishment..." etc. Ahmad said: This question reveals what lies beneath it, namely the obligation to give reasons for the acts of God Almighty, and upon this is built the claim that God may not inflict pain except on the basis of a prior desert, or in anticipation of recompense, or for other considerations of benefit, on the principle held by them regarding what is good and what is best. The children had committed no prior offence and there is no anticipated recompense concerning them, so the question is turned back on that principle. As for the People of the Sunna, God Almighty has undertaken to answer it by His words: "He is not questioned about what He does." This statement refers to the particular event of the people of Noah, and from it the discussion extends to God's ruling on us regarding the enemy: if it is feared that, by fighting them with weapons, their offspring will be harmed, this does not oblige us to refrain from fighting them with destructive and devastating weapons. It is cited as evidence that the Prophet ﷺ shot at the people of al-Ta'if with catapults, and it was said to him concerning them that their offspring were among them, and he said: "They are from their fathers." As for burning them with fire while their offspring are present, Malik, may God have mercy on him, forbade it, except where their harm is feared and they cannot be repelled by other means. And God knows best.]] But they die by various kinds of causes of death, and many of them die by drowning and burning; and this was an added torment for the fathers and mothers as they watched their children drown.

From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "They perish in one destruction and depart by various paths." [[Narrated by Muslim through the chain of Ibn al-Zubayr from Aisha, may God be pleased with her.]] It is also reported from al-Hasan:

that he was asked about this and said: God knew their innocence, so He destroyed them without punishment. It was also said: God made the wombs of their women barren and dried up the loins of their men forty or seventy years before the Flood, so there was no child among them when they drowned.
